narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Bright, clear, and curious (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

teacherGuide.overview: Uses a raindrop to teach reflection, refraction, and lenses, then shows how timing light and sound pulses measures distance.
learningGoals: State that light travels in straight lines.
Describe what a convex lens does and how the eye forms a picture.
Calculate a distance from a timed pulse and its echo.

beforeReading: Put a drop of water on clear plastic over printed text. Ask learners to describe what they see.
whileReading: After Page 2, stand a pencil in a glass of water and view it from the side.
afterReading: Learners draw rays passing through a convex lens to a focus and label the diagram.
discussion: Why is half the time used in every echo calculation? Explain it to a partner.
reflection: Whose work in your community depends on lenses?

mathsExtension.task: Sunlight travels 150,000,000 km to Earth at 300,000 km/s. How long does it take?
An echo sounder hears the echo from a shoal of fish 0.6 seconds after sending the pulse. How deep is the shoal? (Sound: 1,500 m/s.)

support: Provide a ray diagram with the lens already drawn so learners add only the rays.
stretch: Find out the difference between short sight and long sight and which lens corrects each.

factCheck.claim: Speed of light (~300,000 km/s), Moon laser round-trip (~2.56 s for ~384,000 km), and speed of sound in sea water (~1,500 m/s).
factCheck.explanation: Speed of light, Moon distance, and speed of sound in sea water are standard values. The laser round-trip time and the Moon’s drift of about 3.8 cm a year should be confirmed by a science reviewer.
